html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Explain how the scheduler filters, scores and binds
  • Place Pods with node selectors, affinity, taints, tolerations and spread constraints
  • Use priority, QoS classes and eviction order in a scenario
  • Compare the HPA, VPA, Cluster Autoscaler and KEDA

2How the scheduler decides (filter, score, bind), what the exam asks

Running case

Harbor Books Sells More at the Weekend

  • On weekends the shop gets many more visitors, and the storefront must keep up
  • Payment Pods should run on dedicated nodes, and replicas should be spread so one failure does not take the shop down
  • Checkout matters more than the nightly report if the cluster is full
  • In this module you control where Pods go and how many there are

How the Scheduler Decides: Filter, Score, Bind

  • kube-scheduler watches for new Pods with no node
  • Filtering removes nodes that cannot run the Pod, for example nodes without enough free resources for its requests
  • Scoring ranks the remaining nodes, and the highest score wins
  • Binding records the choice with the API server
  • If no node is feasible, the Pod stays unscheduled (Pending)

Exam tip

Filter removes, score ranks, bind records.

What the Exam Asks: Scheduling

  • Filter or score: filtering removes nodes that cannot run the Pod; scoring ranks the rest
  • Affinity or taint: affinity attracts; taints repel; tolerations permit
  • NoSchedule or NoExecute: NoSchedule blocks new Pods; NoExecute also evicts running ones
  • Requests or limits: requests drive placement; limits are enforced
  • QoS order: BestEffort is evicted first, Guaranteed last
  • HPA, VPA or Cluster Autoscaler: more Pods, bigger Pods, or more nodes
Exam tip

For a placement question, ask whether the rule attracts, repels, spreads or ranks.

3NodeSelector, node affinity, pod affinity, taints and tolerations, topology spread, static pods

nodeSelector and Node Affinity

  • nodeSelector is the simplest way to pick nodes: the Pod runs only on nodes whose labels match
  • Node affinity is more expressive, with operators such as In, NotIn, Exists and DoesNotExist
  • required during scheduling is a hard rule; preferred is a soft rule that the scheduler tries to meet
  • If you set both a nodeSelector and node affinity, both must be satisfied

A node selector and a hard node affinity rule

nodeSelector:
  disktype: ssd
affinity:
  nodeAffinity:
    requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          operator: In
          values: [zone-a, zone-b]
Exam tip

required means must, preferred means try.

Pod Affinity and Anti-Affinity

  • Pod affinity places a Pod in a domain that already runs Pods with matching labels
  • Pod anti-affinity keeps it out of such a domain, for example to spread replicas over nodes
  • The topology key, a node label, defines the domain: a node, a rack or a zone
  • These rules look at other Pods' labels, not at node labels, and cost scheduling time in large clusters

Exam tip

Node affinity reads node labels; Pod affinity reads Pod labels.

Taints and Tolerations

  • A taint on a node repels Pods; a toleration on a Pod lets it be placed on a matching tainted node
  • A toleration allows placement but does not guarantee it
  • NoSchedule: no new Pods without a toleration; running Pods stay
  • PreferNoSchedule: the soft version
  • NoExecute: also evicts running Pods that do not tolerate the taint

Exam tip

Taints repel; tolerations permit; NoExecute is the only effect that evicts.

Topology Spread Constraints

  • Topology spread constraints spread Pods across failure domains such as zones and nodes
  • maxSkew: the largest permitted difference in matching Pods between a domain and the domain with the fewest
  • topologyKey names the node label that defines the domains; labelSelector says which Pods count
  • whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule is hard; ScheduleAnyway is soft

Exam tip

Use spread constraints for even distribution; use anti-affinity to keep apart.

Static Pods and Manual Placement Beyond the curriculum

Mechanism What it is
Static Pod a Pod the kubelet runs on one node from manifest files in a folder (staticPodPath); the API server does not manage it, but the kubelet shows a mirror Pod there
nodeName a field that names the node for a Pod directly and skips the scheduler; unusual
  • The main use of static Pods is a self-hosted control plane: components such as the API server run as static Pods
  • The scheduler plays no part in either mechanism
Exam tip

Static Pods belong to one kubelet, not to a controller.

4Priority and preemption, QoS classes and eviction

Priority and Preemption

  • A PriorityClass maps a name to an integer; the higher the value, the more important the Pod
  • A Pod picks one with priorityClassName
  • When a Pod finds no room, the scheduler may preempt: it evicts lower-priority Pods to make space
  • preemptionPolicy: Never stops a Pod from preempting others
  • Values for your own classes go up to one billion; larger ones are reserved for system-cluster-critical and system-node-critical

A class for checkout Pods

apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: checkout-critical
value: 100000
description: Checkout Pods come first
Exam tip

Priority decides who is evicted to make room, not where a Pod goes.

QoS Classes and Eviction

QoS class When Kubernetes assigns it Evicted
Guaranteed every container has CPU and memory requests and limits, and each limit equals its request last
Burstable not Guaranteed, but at least one request or limit is set in the middle
BestEffort no container has any request or limit first
  • Kubernetes assigns the QoS class from a Pod's requests and limits
  • When a node runs out of resources, the kubelet evicts BestEffort, then Burstable, and Guaranteed last
  • The kubelet itself ranks by usage above requests and by priority, so the QoS order is the likely result
Exam tip

No requests and limits means first to go.

5Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, VPA, Cluster Autoscaler, KEDA

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler

  • The HPA changes the number of Pods of a Deployment or StatefulSet to match demand
  • It compares a metric, such as average CPU utilization, with a target
  • Utilization is measured against the Pods' requests; with no requests set, it takes no action
  • Metrics come from the Metrics Server; the HPA checks about every 15 seconds
  • minReplicas and maxReplicas bound the result

Scale the storefront on CPU

kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: {apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: storefront}
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60}
Exam tip

The HPA scales out and in; it needs CPU requests to work.

Other Autoscalers: VPA, Cluster Autoscaler and KEDA Archived topic

  • HPA: more or fewer Pods; VPA: bigger or smaller Pods, by setting requests from usage
  • Cluster Autoscaler: adds nodes when Pods cannot be scheduled, and removes nodes that stay underutilized
  • KEDA (Kubernetes Event Driven Autoscaling) scales workloads from events
  • The Metrics Server feeds the HPA and the VPA

Exam tip

Pods out, Pods up, nodes out: HPA, VPA, Cluster Autoscaler.

6Exam Q&A

6.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1In which order does the kube-scheduler carry out its main steps for a new Pod?

  • AIt scores the nodes, binds the Pod, and then filters out unsuitable nodes
  • BIt binds the Pod to a node, then filters the nodes, and then scores them
  • CIt filters the nodes, binds the Pod to one, and then scores the result
  • DIt filters out unsuitable nodes, scores the rest, and then binds the Pod
Show the answer

Answer: D. The scheduler filters out nodes that cannot run the Pod, scores the feasible ones, and then binds the Pod to the highest-scoring node by telling the API server. Binding comes last.

S2Harbor Books wants other teams' Pods kept off a group of nodes, while the payment Pods are allowed to run there. Which settings do that?

  • AA toleration on the nodes and a taint on the payment Pods
  • BA taint on the nodes and a matching toleration on the payment Pods
  • CA node selector on the other teams' Pods that names the payment nodes
  • DA PriorityClass for the payment Pods that is higher than the others
Show the answer

Answer: B. A taint repels Pods from a node, and a toleration on the payment Pods lets them be placed there. Tolerations belong to Pods and taints to nodes, never the other way round, and a priority does not exclude other Pods from a node.

S3What is the difference between the taint effects NoSchedule and NoExecute?

  • ANoSchedule blocks only new Pods; NoExecute also evicts running Pods that lack a toleration
  • BNoSchedule evicts the running Pods of a node, while NoExecute only blocks new Pods from being placed
  • CThe two effects are identical, and the two names differ only by the Kubernetes version that uses them
  • DNoSchedule applies to Pods, while NoExecute applies only to the nodes of one particular cluster
Show the answer

Answer: A. NoSchedule stops new Pods that do not tolerate the taint but leaves running Pods alone. NoExecute also evicts running Pods that do not tolerate it. PreferNoSchedule is the soft version.

S4A Deployment's replicas must be spread across three zones, so that no zone holds more than one Pod more than the emptiest zone. Which setting does this?

  • AA node selector that names one zone for the replicas of the Deployment
  • BA taint on the nodes of each zone, with the effect NoExecute set on each of the taints
  • CA topology spread constraint with a maxSkew of one and a zone topology key
  • DA PriorityClass with the highest value that a user-defined class may have
Show the answer

Answer: C. A topology spread constraint spreads matching Pods across domains, and maxSkew sets the largest allowed difference, here one, with the zone label as the topology key. A node selector would pin all replicas to one zone, and taints and priorities do not distribute Pods.

S5A node runs short of memory. Which Pods does the kubelet evict first?

  • AGuaranteed Pods, because they hold the largest memory reservations
  • BBestEffort Pods, because they have no requests or limits at all
  • CBurstable Pods, because they are always the newest Pods on a node
  • DStatic Pods, because the API server does not manage them
Show the answer

Answer: B. Under node pressure the usual order is BestEffort Pods first, then Burstable ones, and Guaranteed Pods last; the kubelet ranks by usage above requests and then priority, which gives this order in the usual case. Age and static Pods do not decide it.

S6Checkout Pods must keep running, even if less important batch Pods have to be evicted when the cluster is full. What gives them that ability?

  • AA ResourceQuota for the shop namespace with a high CPU ceiling
  • BA higher CPU limit on the checkout containers than on the batch ones
  • CA nodeName that places the checkout Pods on the largest worker node
  • DA PriorityClass with a higher value, which the checkout Pods select
Show the answer

Answer: D. A higher priority lets the scheduler preempt lower-priority Pods to place the checkout Pods. A quota caps a namespace, a CPU limit does not change eviction order for the scheduler, and nodeName bypasses scheduling without freeing any room.

S7The storefront HPA targets 60% average CPU utilization, but it never scales the Deployment. Which cause is likely?

  • AThe containers set no CPU request, so the utilization is not defined
  • BThe Deployment uses the RollingUpdate strategy instead of Recreate
  • CThe nodes carry too few labels for the scheduler to read them correctly
  • DThe Pods have a QoS class of Guaranteed and so can never be scaled
Show the answer

Answer: A. CPU utilization is measured against the Pods' requests, so with no request the HPA has nothing to compute and takes no action. The update strategy, node labels and the QoS class do not stop an HPA.

S8Pods stay Pending because no node has enough free CPU, and the cluster runs in a cloud. Which component adds nodes?

  • AThe Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, which adds Pods when CPU use is high
  • BThe Vertical Pod Autoscaler, which resizes the requests of the Pods
  • CThe Cluster Autoscaler, which adds nodes when Pods find no room
  • DThe kube-proxy on each node, which balances the load between nodes
Show the answer

Answer: C. The Cluster Autoscaler adjusts the number of nodes when Pods cannot be scheduled for lack of resources, and removes nodes that stay underutilized. The HPA changes Pod counts and the VPA changes requests.

S9Which autoscaler sets the CPU and memory requests of a Pod from its observed usage?

  • AThe Vertical Pod Autoscaler, which works from the usage it observes
  • BThe Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, which works from metrics such as CPU
  • CThe Cluster Autoscaler, which works from Pods that cannot be scheduled
  • DKEDA, which works from events that it is configured to watch
Show the answer

Answer: A. The VPA sets requests from observed usage. The HPA changes the number of Pods, the Cluster Autoscaler changes the number of nodes, and KEDA scales workloads from events.

7Quick Reference Card

Static Pods run by one kubelet from manifest files
